Saving Private Ryan should be relegated to the category of okay movie. After almost thirty years since my original viewing, it is hard to remember why this film was so lauded. I remember as a kid the theater being completely silent when it concluded, patrons with heads hung low, shuffling out in remembrance of what was lost and won. In retrospect it seems like it received such critical praise and accolades because the greatest generation was dying off and guilt did the rest of the work. Somehow Spielberg won Best Directing over Terrence Malick's The Thin Red Line, released the same year and a better film by every measure. I will give Saving Private Ryan Best Sound, Sound Editing, and Cinematography, but none of those awards require Spielberg. He directed a boring story that generates so much momentum in the first twenty minutes from the iconic D-Day landing that the energy alone carries you across the finish line. The rest of the film is a ragtag bunch of Rangers looking for Private Ryan, and just like Tom Hanks' squad asking why they are hunting for him, I too was wondering why this movie deserves praise for a boring fetch quest with no compelling answer as to why anyone cares about Ryan outside of his mother. The acting ranges from meh to okay. Part of the problem is Spielberg created tropes for characters. None of them felt real. The Rudy character as a scared soldier with a heart of gold, the rough around the edges guy from Brooklyn who means well once you get to know him. Maybe my age or internet-saturated storytelling has ruined my patience for this, but they mostly felt one-dimensional and wooden with zero character development across the entire runtime. My biggest gripe is the ending, which plays like a video game. Characters have plot armor that lets them run through bullets fired from fifty different Nazis, artillery strikes, and flak cannons without a scratch, unless the plot demands otherwise. About ten Americans with limited resources take on a battalion of Nazis with multiple tanks in their own WWII Battle of Thermopylae, fighting over a bridge that could be repaired in a week but is somehow of vital importance. The most egregious part is that each main American soldier kills approximately fifty Nazis apiece, as hoards of Germans seek out American bullets like moths to a flame. I was rolling my eyes. Bad writing, bad directing, and I am scratching my head as to why this was considered good even by 1998 standards. Saving Private Ryan is the cinematic equivalent of the books your English teacher forced you to read in high school. The same false arbiters of culture who decided Wuthering Heights and Slaughterhouse-Five must be preserved for future generations have decided this film is sacred. Saving Private Ryan is patriotism bordering on jingoism dressed up as prestige cinema.

Spielberg works his magic once again. The first 30 minutes or so of this film are masterfully shot, written, acted, and edited. It’s a genuinely unflinching, brutal, and deeply heartbreaking depiction of World War II that I have not seen anything like. The pain, the horror of it all, is ridiculously intense and it really puts things into perspective. The cinematography throughout is absolutely breathtaking, using natural landscapes, framing, and camera motion to perfectly capture the various emotions of the film. Tom Hanks delivers the standout performance here. I grow continually more impressed with his acting range and how he is able to portray such complex characters so well. Matt Damon is also great, as usual, and the supporting cast in general is very good as well. The storyline is extremely compelling (bring Matt Damon home 🤯) and results in an emotional, epic journey for a small squad of soldiers searching for one man. It truly feels like an epic journey in so many ways. I wouldn’t have minded if it was maybe just a half-hour shorter, as I found some of the really powerful moments not to be the loud, chaotic combat scenes, but the smaller-scale, intense interactions between soldiers just trying to keep surviving and getting through these traumatic experiences. There is a great amount of both, but my only real complaint with this movie is that it feels a bit long in parts. However, that’s a small nitpick in what is otherwise a ridiculously entertaining, important film that is masterfully made. There’s a reason that Spielberg is considered one of the best to ever do it. His range as a director is simply remarkable. He can create lighthearted, family friendly crowd pleasers like ET and then turn around and deliver a haunting, gorgeously shot war epic that captures the horrors of World War II.

This was such an easy 5 stars before some truly baffling creative decisions. The crude humor during moments of genuine mortal tension repeatedly pulled me out of the film. I understand what the characterization of Upham is doing and why he behaves the way he does, but frankly, I couldn’t care less. Everything about him repulsed me: the cowardice, the naïveté, his constant glorification of war, and especially the fact that he repeats what the film itself frames as a mistake by releasing more prisoners. And why have Steamboat come back? What exactly was the message there? Was it to suggest that you shouldn’t spare your enemies? That good deeds sometimes don’t go unpunished? Or that you should continue doing good despite that possibility? If it was the latter, I don’t think the film communicates it particularly well. And that’s what makes this so frustrating. This is still a fantastic movie. I had a genuinely great time watching it. Tom Hanks is stellar as ever, the plot is compelling, and the cinematography and action sequences are incredible. But man, I genuinely can’t remember the last time a film irritated me this much.

That opening battle might be one of the most insane things I’ve ever watched. Spielberg doesn’t make D-Day look exciting or heroic in the normal movie sense. People are drowning before they even reach the beach, bullets are ripping through soldiers, explosions make Miller temporarily lose his hearing, and medics are trying to save people who are already basically dead. The shaky camera, washed-out look, sound, and complete confusion make it feel like Spielberg is dropping you into the middle of Omaha Beach instead of letting you comfortably watch it. What surprised me is that the rest of the movie is much quieter. The mission to save Ryan sounds heroic until the soldiers start questioning why eight men should risk their lives for one person they don’t even know. Tom Hanks is perfect as Miller because he never feels like some unstoppable war hero. He’s exhausted, scared, his hand won’t stop shaking, and he’s just trying to keep his men together long enough to finish the mission. Wade’s death and Mellish getting slowly stabbed were especially hard to watch. I do think the movie loses a little momentum between the opening and final battle, but when that last battle starts Spielberg somehow manages to make everything feel chaotic while still letting me understand where everyone is and what they’re trying to do. “Earn this” is such a brutal thing for Ryan to have to carry for the rest of his life. After *Schindler’s List* and now this, Spielberg might be even better when he takes away all the spectacle and forces you to look directly at people.

I have empathy for everyone who has been to war. That being said, it must take an extraordinary amount of courage to go to war knowing that you may very well die and that survival itself can feel like a miracle. A forma como Spielberg retrata a guerra é tão realista e intimista que mostra que os soldados não são heróis invencíveis, mas humanos. A cena mais memorável, pra mim, é o momento em que, antes de acontecer o ataque mais violento do filme, os soldados restantes ouvem  e cantam "Tu est partout", da Édith Piaf, em um gramofone improvisado no meio das ruínas. Isso humaniza eles, de certa forma, e rompe com o silêncio opressivo antes do ataque. Eles meio que deixam de serem soldados e voltam a serem civis, com famílias, casas, sonhos. Além disso, a cena em que Upham fica travado na escada no dilema de subir ou não, por mais que possa dar ao público um ar de covardia vindo do tradutor, é extremamente realista. Diante de soldados corajosos e acostumados com o caos da guerra, Upham representava a inocência do grupo, tendo até defendido um soldado alemão antes. A paralisia ao entregar as munições enquanto um americano morria no andar de cima mostra que Spielberg desmitifica o heroísmo de todos os soldados da guerra, retratando também o medo. A reação de Upham representa, mesmo que estressando o público, a reação mais provável e humana de um civil jogado em um combate. Eu até lembrei, na hora, do Dae-Ho, em Squid Game, que tem uma reação idêntica à essa, ficando paralisado e em pânico ao ter que entregar as munições ao grupo durante a rebelião. Uma reação completamente humana. Por fim, a reação de Upham acaba o humilhando, quando os soldados alemães passam por ele e nem atacam, mostrando que eles não o vêem como uma ameaça. E o desfecho é que ele acaba cometendo um crime de guerra, matando o soldado alemçao que ele mesmo havia insistido pra ficar, como forma de vingança ao Capitão Miller. Spielberg mostra como a guerra corrompe, até mesmo a pessoa mais inocente do grupo. A guerra tira a humanidade dos soldados.

Saving Private Ryan é um daqueles filmes que conseguem fazer a guerra parecer algo físico. Não é só assistir aos personagens lutando; existe uma sensação constante de caos, medo e desorientação. A sequência inicial do desembarque na Normandia é provavelmente uma das representações mais impactantes de combate que já vi. Spielberg não tenta transformar aquilo em uma batalha "bonita". A câmera fica próxima dos soldados, o som é agressivo e tudo acontece de maneira extremamente caótica. Também gosto bastante de como o filme equilibra as grandes cenas de batalha com momentos mais silenciosos entre os personagens. A missão de encontrar Ryan funciona como uma estrutura para discutir o custo humano da guerra e o significado de sacrificar algumas vidas para salvar uma pessoa. Tom Hanks funciona muito bem como Miller porque ele não é apresentado como um super-herói. É um homem tentando cumprir uma missão enquanto carrega o peso de tudo que está acontecendo ao redor. É um filme longo, mas a direção mantém a tensão muito bem construída. Um clássico do gênero e, pra mim, facilmente 5 estrelas.

“Earn this.” The famous final words of Tom Hanks’ Captain Miller as he dies on the bridge at the end of Saving Private Ryan. I don’t think we fully comprehend what we have when it comes to freedom in the United States. Captain Miller and his band of brothers embark on a mission to save just one soldier, and one by one, they sacrifice themselves to secure his freedom and his future. As Miller lies dying, his final words to Private Ryan are simple: “Earn this.” That phrase feels increasingly distant from the hearts and minds of Americans today. What are we supposed to earn? Most of us honestly don’t know. We have grown up surrounded by freedoms of every kind, so completely immersed in them that it can be difficult to imagine another reality—one in which those freedoms are absent, restricted, or taken away entirely. Freedom can never be treated as something guaranteed. It requires vigilance, but it also requires something more: responsibility toward one another. We inherit a country and a way of life purchased, time and time again, through the sacrifices of people we will never meet. I hope that, in brotherhood and sisterhood, we can continue striving to earn this—not because freedom should have to be earned as a condition of possessing it, but because sacrifice deserves remembrance, gratitude, and a willingness to leave something worthy behind for the generations that follow us. One of the greatest films ever made. In nearly every way, Saving Private Ryan is a masterpiece.
